Unofficial connector, not affiliated with Envertech. It reads your Envertech
EVT800 micro-inverter on your home network, through its local TCP link,
without any cloud and without any account.

**Never tested with a real device**: it was built from the pyenvertechevt800
library (the one Home Assistant uses) and the frames of its tests. The
protocol is not documented by Envertech. Please report what you see (see
"Feedback" below).

## What you get

One Gladys device per micro-inverter, named after its serial number:

| Feature                      | What it is                                                                              |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Solar production (W)         | the power of all its inputs together; 0 at night                                        |
| Solar production index (kWh) | a cumulative index for the Gladys energy monitoring (production per half hour, revenue) |
| Inverter online              | 1 while the inverter sends its frames, 0 asleep (the night)                             |
| AC voltage (V)               | the grid voltage the inverter sees                                                      |
| Grid frequency (Hz)          | a plain number (Gladys has no Hz unit)                                                  |
| Input n power (W)            | the power of each input (one panel each)                                                |
| Input n DC voltage (V)       | the voltage of the panel                                                                |
| Input n DC current (A)       | the current of the panel (power divided by voltage)                                     |
| Input n temperature (°C)     | the temperature the inverter gives for that input                                       |

Read-only: the integration only acknowledges the frames of the inverter (as
the library does, the inverter expects it), it never sends a command. The
inverter gives no counter of the day; its lifetime counter per input is not
published on its own (see "The energy index").

## Setting it up

1. The EVT800 must be in its "TCP server" mode (the mode the Home Assistant
   integration uses), listening on port 14889. Find its IP address in your
   router and give it a fixed address if you can.
2. In Gladys, open the integration, enter the address (by day: at night the
   inverter is powered off with its panels), and save. Add `:port` only if it
   is not 14889.
3. Open the "Discover" tab and create the device. Its values come with the
   next frame of the inverter.
4. Optional: enter the peak power of the panels on this inverter (kWp). It
   bounds what the energy index may take between two frames (2 kW when
   empty). Never enter less than the real peak power: in doubt, leave it
   empty.

The integration keeps one connection open and publishes the last frame at
most once a minute. It never tries to connect more than once a minute,
whatever asks (a restart, a save, the test button). The "Test the
connection" button tells the last frame, or makes the connection attempt when
one is due and waits for the first frame.

If another program (Home Assistant, for example) is connected to the
inverter at the same time, the inverter may refuse the second connection:
use one of them. Such a refusal cannot be told from the night: by day, the
status then says "asleep" (and mentions this case).

The link is kept only by data frames of the inverter it first answered with:
without one for 90 s, it is closed and tried again at the pace, and the
inverter is shown offline. Frames of another serial number on the same
connection are ignored; another inverter at the address (a new connection)
gets its own device.

## The night

An EVT800 is powered by its panels: at sunset it stops and goes silent. That
is not an error: after three failed attempts with a power under 20 W (or an
hour of silence whatever the power), the inverter is "asleep", its powers go
to 0, the status stays green and says so, and it is tried every 5 minutes
until it wakes up. The status turns red (the inverter shown offline) if the
inverter vanishes while producing 20 W or more (new tries after 1 minute,
doubled up to 15 minutes),
if the address does not give EVT800 frames, or if there is no frame for more
than a day.

While the status is red after a link lost in production, the powers keep
their last value in Gladys (never 0 by day: the integration does not know
them); only "Inverter online" goes to 0. A scene that relies on the power
should also check "Inverter online". After an hour, the inverter is asleep
and the powers go to 0.

## The energy index

Each input of the inverter has its own lifetime counter. The production index
is their sum, published only when every input gives its counter (a partial
sum would look like a drop, then a jump). It goes through a guard: it is
never 0; a jump larger than the peak power allows since the last value, or a
drop, is held back, shown in the integration status, and only taken when you
click "Accept the held index" in the configuration (a jump is then counted at
once; nothing is counted for a drop, the index goes on from there). Saving
the configuration never accepts anything.

During a night that follows a low power, the reference of the guard is dated
again at every attempt: in the morning, the margin counts from the night, not
from the evening, so a wrong first frame is held.

It is not known whether the EVT800 keeps its counters when it powers up in
the morning. If every counter is lower right after such a night, by no more
than the margin since the wake-up, the integration takes it as a reset: the
index goes on from its value (the counters of the evening are added to it,
as the Zeversolar and Imeon integrations chain their counter of the day).
If the old counters come back within 3 hours, the reset is undone and
nothing is counted twice. A drop by day is still held. If a drop is held
every morning anyway, do not accept it each day: please report it.

When the device gains an input (updated in Discovery), the index goes on from
its value: the old counter of the new input is never counted.

## Limits

- One micro-inverter per integration; two inputs at most (as the library).
- The protocol is not documented: the meaning of each value comes from the
  library, checked only against the frames of its tests.
- The integration needs Gladys 5.2.0 or later.

## Privacy

Nothing leaves your network: the integration only talks to the address you
entered. Only the serial number, the number of inputs, the night, the index
state (guard and counters) and the times of the last attempt and frame are
kept in `/data`.

## Feedback

Issues and pull requests: [https://github.com/LM1LC3N7/gladys-envertech](https://github.com/LM1LC3N7/gladys-envertech). If
you own an EVT800, the integration logs (by day and at night, with the serial
numbers hidden) help a lot.

## Configuration settings

These are the settings Envertech asks for in its configuration screen in Gladys.

| Setting | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Envertech micro-inverter | `section` | No | Unofficial connector, not affiliated with Envertech. It reads an Envertech EVT800 micro-inverter on your network, without any cloud, through its local TCP link ("TCP server" mode, port 14889): solar power, power, voltage, current and temperature of each input, AC voltage, grid frequency, and a solar production index for the Gladys energy monitoring (the lifetime counters of the inputs). At night the inverter sleeps: the power goes to 0. Read-only: it only acknowledges the frames of the inverter, never a command. The protocol is not documented by Envertech. Never tested with a real Envertech inverter. |
| Inverter address | `string` | Yes | The IP address of the EVT800 on your network (shown by your router), with a port only if it is not 14889. Enter it by day: at night the inverter sleeps and does not answer. Preferably give it a fixed address in your router. |
| Peak power of the panels (kWp, optional) | `number` | No | The peak power of the panels on this inverter. It bounds what the energy index may take between two frames (an odd frame is held back instead). Empty: 2 kW. Never enter less than the real peak power: in doubt, leave it empty. |

## How to install Envertech in Gladys

1. In Gladys, open **Integrations**: Envertech appears in the catalog, next to the native integrations, with a community badge.
2. Click **Install**. Gladys pulls the Docker image (`ghcr.io/lm1lc3n7/gladys-envertech:0.1.4`), starts it in a sandbox isolated from the core, and generates the integration's interface (devices, discovery and configuration).
3. Open the **Configuration** screen of the integration, fill in the settings, and save.
4. You can also install it directly from its repository URL: [https://github.com/LM1LC3N7/gladys-envertech](https://github.com/LM1LC3N7/gladys-envertech).

Envertech requires Gladys `>=5.2.0`. The catalog inside Gladys refreshes every hour, so a new version becomes available at most one hour after its release.

Not running Gladys yet? It is free and open source: [follow the installation guide](/docs/) to get started.

## About external integrations

Envertech is an **external integration**: a community integration packaged as a Docker container and published on GitHub, that Gladys installs in one click and runs in a sandbox isolated from its core. It is published and maintained by [LM1LC3N7](https://github.com/LM1LC3N7), not by the Gladys core team.
